chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
title: Black composers of the day and Jelly Roll Morton's claim on 'St. Louis Blues'
summary: The only Black composers he knew were Piron and Clarence Williams; he thinks Jelly Roll wrote 'St. Louis Blues' and recounts how Jelly Roll got advances from Melrose by writing tunes.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Because at that time there weren't many or weren't any colored composers with published works?
Not -- Only ones I knew was Piron, A. J. Piron and Clarence Williams.
That's the only ones I knew. I didn't
know Scott Joplin or W. C. Handy, none of them.
Handy's works were published then, were they?
What -- I don't remember when they were first published.
No, neither was Jelly Roll's. Jelly Roll swore he's the composer of 'St. Louis Blues.' He said the old man stole it, he said, but since he made people think he did it, let him have the glory.
Do you think Jelly Roll wrote it?
Yeah, I think so. Excuse me.

Jelly Roll wrote a lot of things. Every time he wanted something he used to -- Melrose used to publish his pieces, you know, and every time he wanted $1,000, $2,000, or anything he'd write up a tune and give it to Melrose and say, 'Give me some advance money.' And that's how he used to get his money. And he had a diamond in his tooth in front there and he was a pimp, and he can talk himself into a job and talk himself out of it. He was quite a guy.
You knew him in New York?
I knew him -- Yeah, sure. He was quite a guy.
